blocks.text: A useful way of representing electronic configurations is a diagram that places electrons in boxes Figure 2.13.

items: Each box represents an atomic orbital.
The boxes (orbitals) can be arranged in order of increasing energy from bottom to top.
An electron is represented by an arrow.

blocks.text: The direction of the arrow represents the ‘spin’ of the electron.
When there are two electrons in an orbital, the ‘spins’ of the electrons are opposite, so the two arrows in this box point in opposite direction.

blocks.alt: Boron in boxes, arranged from bottom to top: 1s with a pair of opposite arrows, 2s with a pair of opposite arrows, and 2p as three boxes with one upward arrow in the first and the other two empty.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.13: The electronic configuration of boron in boxes (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.13).

blocks.text: Electrons in the same region of space repel each other because they have the same charge. So wherever possible, electrons will occupy separate orbitals in the same subshell to minimize this repulsion. These electrons have the same ‘spins’ in different orbitals. Electrons are only paired when there are no more empty orbitals available within a subshell.
Figure 2.14 shows the electronic structures of carbon, nitrogen and oxygen to illustrate these points

blocks.alt: Box diagrams for carbon (1s2 2s2 2p2), nitrogen (1s2 2s2 2p3) and oxygen (1s2 2s2 2p4). Carbon has single arrows in two of the three 2p boxes, nitrogen single arrows in all three, and oxygen a pair in 2px with single arrows in 2py and 2pz: electrons pair only when every orbital already has one.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.14: When adding electrons to a particular subshell, the electrons are only paired when no more empty orbitals are available (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.14).
